meta.date: ~600 BC (first year of the reign of Zedekiah)

world_behind.title: A new king under Babylon's hand
world_behind.text: The chapter dates itself "in the commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah" (v. 4). Zedekiah was Judah's last king, installed by Babylon after a first deportation had already carried off his predecessor and thousands of Jerusalem's leading families. A householder of Lehi's standing had watched neighbors disappear eastward. The prophets' warning was not exotic speculation; it was the visible trajectory of the kingdom.

cites.quote: in the commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah

spans.text: in the commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah

world_behind.title: Many prophets, one message
world_behind.text: In that same year "there came many prophets, prophesying unto the people that they must repent" (v. 4). Jeremiah's ministry was running through these exact years, and his book preserves the same city-wide argument over the same message. Lehi enters the story as one voice in a chorus, which is how Nephi presents him: not the era's lone visionary but a man who joined the warning and then saw for himself.

cites.quote: there came many prophets, prophesying unto the people that they must repent

spans.text: there came many prophets, prophesying unto the people that they must repent

world_behind.title: Lehi's household and means
world_behind.text: Lehi had "dwelt at Jerusalem in all his days)" (v. 4), and the next chapters show a family of substance: gold, silver, and a land of inheritance worth returning for (1 Ne. 3:16, 22). A house that could school a son in two literacies was not a poor one. Perhaps the Egyptian came by trade down the caravan routes; the record never says, only that the learning was there when it was needed.

cites.quote: dwelt at Jerusalem in all his days)

spans.text: dwelt at Jerusalem in all his days)

world_behind.title: Two schoolings in one boy
world_behind.text: Nephi writes in "the learning of the Jews and the language of the Egyptians" (v. 2): scripture and script, a religious education and a professional one. Whatever the exact writing system, the claim tells us record-making was a taught craft in this family before it became a commandment.

cites.quote: the learning of the Jews and the language of the Egyptians

spans.text: the learning of the Jews and the language of the Egyptians

world_behind.title: Written a generation later
world_behind.text: This page was engraved roughly thirty years after the family left the city; the small plates begin that late (2 Ne. 5:28–31), in another land, by a writer who already knows how the story ends. The calm of the opening sentence is a survivor's calm, and the gratitude in it is retrospective.

world_behind.title: Killing the messenger was recent practice
world_behind.text: Jeremiah stood trial for preaching exactly this doom, and the same account records a prophet named Urijah hunted into Egypt and executed for it (Jer. 26). The plot against Lehi's life (v. 20) is not narrative color; it is what that city, in those years, did with that sermon.

words.text: In the record's older English, goodly leans toward substance and standing as much as virtue: parents of means and reputation, the kind of household that could afford the double schooling of v. 2. The word lets Nephi honor his parents without flattering them; what they are in this sentence is the reason he was "taught somewhat in all the learning of my father" (v. 1).

cites.quote: taught somewhat in all the learning of my father

spans.text: taught somewhat in all the learning of my father

words.text: Twice in two verses Lehi is "overcome with the Spirit" (v. 7): he comes home from a vision and collapses onto his bed, and it is while "thus overcome" (v. 8) that the greater vision opens. The record treats the body's giving-out not as weakness but as a doorway; the second sight begins exactly where his strength ends.

cites.quote: overcome with the Spirit

spans.text: overcome with the Spirit

cites.quote: thus overcome

spans.text: thus overcome

words.text: A concourse is a running-together, a crowd in motion. Heaven in Lehi's first look is not a still courtroom but "numberless concourses of angels in the attitude of singing and praising their God" (v. 8) — assembly, movement, and music before any word is spoken to him.

cites.quote: numberless concourses of angels in the attitude of singing and praising their God

spans.text: numberless concourses of angels in the attitude of singing and praising their God

words.text: The One who descends has "luster" (v. 9) beyond "the sun at noon-day" (v. 9), and the twelve who follow exceed "the stars in the firmament" (v. 10). The measures are homely, the two brightnesses everyone has stood under, and they rank the scene: one light above them all, twelve below it, the story's whole order of authority given as light before anyone is named.

words.text: A working scribe's word. To abridge is to choose, and Nephi says so on his first page: "I make an abridgment of the record of my father" (v. 17). The reader is warned at the door that selection is happening — that a larger book of Lehi exists and that we will get it only through his son's editing hand.

cites.quote: I make an abridgment of the record of my father

spans.text: I make an abridgment of the record of my father

phrases.text: Three times in three verses: "I make a record of my proceedings" (v. 1), "I make a record in the language of my father" (v. 2), and "the record which I make is true" (v. 3). The opening is a maker's mark: what this object is, whose hand made it, in what language, and on what warrant, all set down before any event is narrated. The book is about records before it is about anyone's story.

spans.text: I make a record in the language of my father

phrases.term: the learning of the Jews and the language of the Egyptians
phrases.text: A deliberate pairing: sacred learning in one column, a borrowed writing system in the other. Centuries on, the record's last editor will explain the choice in practical terms — Egyptian characters take less room on metal than Hebrew would (Morm. 9:32–33). The strange hybrid announced here is what makes a thousand-year engraved library possible.

Exodus's sign for God leading a nation by night, and here it "dwelt upon a rock" (v. 6) before a single praying man. The national symbol arrives at personal scale, and what follows is an exodus in miniature: one family led out of a doomed city into a wilderness toward a promised land.

cites.quote: dwelt upon a rock

spans.text: dwelt upon a rock

phrases.text: The phrase Lehi reads in the book is the phrase the histories would use of the event itself — Jeremiah's narrative deploys it word for word (Jer. 39:9). Inside this volume it keeps resurfacing: Lehi preaches it again (1 Ne. 10:3), and Amaleki dates the Mulekites' escape by it (Omni 1:15). A sentence of prophecy hardening into a date-stamp.

phrases.term: Great and marvelous are thy works
phrases.text: Lehi's outburst lands almost verbatim in the hymn John hears the redeemed sing (Rev. 15:3). Either heavenly praise has a shared register across the books, or Lehi — fresh from hearing the concourses sing — is already talking the way heaven talks. The record lets both readings stand.

Psalm diction (Ps. 25:6), but Nephi's use of it is not a sigh but a claim with a demonstration attached: "I, Nephi, will show unto you" (v. 20). The gentlest phrase in the chapter is doing the hardest work in the book: naming the thesis every later deliverance will be called to prove.

cites.quote: I, Nephi, will show unto you

spans.text: I, Nephi, will show unto you

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: Afflictions and favor in one breath
verses.text: The first sentence holds "having seen many afflictions" (v. 1) and "having been highly favored of the Lord in all my days" (v. 1) together without explaining how both can be true. Four "having" clauses stack a whole life into the opening line, and the tension they refuse to resolve — hard days, favored days, the same days — is the tension the entire record will keep working.

cites.quote: having seen many afflictions

spans.text: having seen many afflictions

cites.quote: having been highly favored of the Lord in all my days

spans.text: having been highly favored of the Lord in all my days

verses.label: v. 4
verses.title: Dated to a public crisis
verses.text: Nephi pins the family story to a regnal year and a street full of prophets. It is the only verse of background the chapter allows itself, and it does double work: it starts the book's clock, and it places Lehi's private vision inside a public argument already underway.

verses.label: v. 5–6
verses.title: Intercession comes first
verses.text: Lehi's first recorded act is prayer "with all his heart, in behalf of his people" (v. 5). The pillar of fire interrupts a man already pleading for the city that will shortly want him dead. The order is worth keeping: compassion precedes commission, and the vision finds him mid-prayer, not mid-doubt.

cites.quote: with all his heart, in behalf of his people

spans.text: with all his heart, in behalf of his people

verses.label: v. 8–10
verses.title: The opened heavens, ranked by light
verses.text: God enthroned amid singing; then One descending whose brightness beats the noon sun; then twelve who outshine stars. Even the grammar is careful: "he thought he saw" (v. 8). The son refuses to state more than his source claimed. Readers reach ch. 11 before the Twelve are seen again and the scene begins to be explained (1 Ne. 11:29).

cites.quote: he thought he saw

spans.text: he thought he saw

verses.label: v. 11–12
verses.title: The book does the filling
verses.text: The first figure hands Lehi not a staff or a sword but "a book, and bade him that he should read" (v. 11); and it is "as he read" (v. 12) that he "was filled with the Spirit of the Lord" (v. 12). In a chapter obsessed with records, heaven's own chosen instrument is a text, and reading is the act that carries the Spirit in.

verses.label: v. 14–15
verses.title: The arc ends in praise
verses.text: The man who quaked and trembled at v. 6 is exclaiming "Great and marvelous are thy works" (v. 14) by v. 14, and his "soul did rejoice" (v. 15). A vision of his city's ruin produces, of all things, worship, because behind the ruin he was shown mercy: "thou wilt not suffer those who come unto thee that they shall perish" (v. 14).

verses.label: v. 18–20
verses.title: The refusal, and the answer
verses.text: Lehi obeys and preaches; Jerusalem answers with mockery and a plot. Then the chapter does something strange: mid-crisis, with his father's life in danger, Nephi turns to the reader and promises a demonstration: "to make them mighty even unto the power of deliverance" (v. 20). The moral is placed before the story that will earn it, a title hung over everything that follows.

cites.quote: to make them mighty even unto the power of deliverance

spans.text: to make them mighty even unto the power of deliverance

chapter.title: A record that explains itself first
chapter.text: Verses 1–3 and 16–17 form a frame around the vision: provenance, language, the maker's own hand, a truth-claim, and an editorial method, stated before and after the story they enclose. The book opens the way an archive opens, with a label, and the label's confidence ("I know that the record which I make is true" (v. 3)) is itself part of what the book asks the reader to test.

cites.quote: I know that the record which I make is true

spans.text: I know that the record which I make is true

chapter.title: The prophet's call, minus the protest
chapter.text: Set beside the scenes it resembles — Micaiah's throne and host (1 Kgs. 22:19), Isaiah's temple vision (Isa. 6), Ezekiel handed a scroll (Ezek. 2) — Lehi's call has every classic element but one: the objection. No slow tongue, no unclean lips, no "I am a child." His answer to the vision is praise, and his answer to the commission is going (v. 18). The chapter shows the pattern landing on a heart that does not argue back.

chapter.title: The thesis before the evidence
chapter.text: Verse 20 converts the book from a chronicle into a demonstration: Nephi names what all of it will show, tender mercies reaching the faithful with power to deliver, before a single deliverance has happened. First-time readers meet the claim; everything afterward arrives as evidence.

chapter.title: Father and son hold each other up
chapter.text: Opening with Lehi's call gives Nephi's record its authority: the son writes as witness to a witness. But the dependence runs both ways: Lehi's book survives only inside the abridgment (v. 16–17). The father makes the son credible; the son makes the father last.

chapter.title: A preface in a hurry
chapter.text: Twenty verses carry a theophany, a heavenly book, a commission, and a murder plot, while a single later vision will get whole chapters. Twice Nephi says he is not making "a full account" (v. 16). The speed is a signal: this chapter is a doorway, built to reach its thesis fast, not the room the book will live in.

cites.quote: a full account

spans.text: a full account

chapter.title: Opening the departure unit
chapter.text: Chapters 2–7 hang from hooks set here: the announced destruction drives the flight into the wilderness (ch. 2), the family's regard for records sends the sons back for the brass plates (chs. 3–4), and the doomed city gives the second return its urgency (ch. 7). The unit keeps orbiting what this chapter planted.

chapter.title: The first editor shows his method
chapter.text: The plan of vv. 16–17, to abridge the father's record and then give his own account, is the volume's working pattern in miniature. Mormon will do to a thousand years of records what Nephi does here to Lehi's book, and both tell the reader plainly that they are doing it.

applications.title: Write what you can vouch for
applications.text: Nephi's opening standard is narrow and strong: his own proceedings, his own hand, his own knowledge. A personal record built that way — things seen and known, not things repeated — is small at first and permanent after. Start the page with what you could sign.

applications.title: Intercede before you criticize
applications.text: Lehi earns his hard sermon in prayer, "with all his heart, in behalf of his people" (v. 5), before he ever preaches it. The practice transfers directly: pray for the group you are about to correct — family, ward, city — and notice what the praying does to the correcting.

cites.quote: with all his heart, in behalf of his people

spans.text: with all his heart, in behalf of his people

applications.title: Read expecting to be filled
applications.text: The Spirit reached Lehi through an act of reading. Treat that as a mechanic, not a marvel: bring the book, read while the heart is soft from prayer, and let the reading — not the mood before it — be the vehicle.

applications.title: Let praise finish the arc
applications.text: Lehi's encounter runs fear to worship inside ten verses. Audit your own hard news: where does the arc stop — at the quaking, or at "thy power, and goodness, and mercy are over all the inhabitants of the earth" (v. 14)? The destination is a choice, and it can be practiced.

cites.quote: thy power, and goodness, and mercy are over all the inhabitants of the earth

spans.text: thy power, and goodness, and mercy are over all the inhabitants of the earth

applications.title: Expect old answers to old truth
applications.text: The mocking Lehi drew was "even as with the prophets of old" (v. 20): a rerun, not a referendum. When a true thing you carry gets the standard reception, read it as the pattern holding, and hold with it.

cites.quote: even as with the prophets of old

spans.text: even as with the prophets of old

applications.title: Keep a tender-mercies ledger
applications.text: Nephi does not say the Lord is merciful; he says he will show it. Keep the same discipline for a year: a running list of specific, dated mercies. The claim becomes yours the way it became his — by exhibits.

questions.text: Where in my life do "many afflictions" and "highly favored" describe the same stretch of days, and which name do I reach for first when I tell that story?
When warnings multiply around me, do I hear many prophets or background noise, and what would make me check?
Whom do I pray for with all my heart, and is that circle any bigger than my own house?
What was the last thing I read that filled me, and what do I keep reading that never could?
After hard counsel or hard news, how long before my language turns to praise, and what does it turn to instead?
What record am I abridging — which parts of my parents' story am I responsible to carry forward, and am I carrying them?
If I had to show, not tell, the tender mercies of the Lord in my own year, what would I put in evidence?
